en: Preface to the *Xifang queshi* (Direct Pointing to the West):
In the summer of the Dingwei year, I visited the abbot’s quarters of Master Xueshan. The Master produced a book and handed it to me, saying, "This is a precious raft.
Moreover, its origins are most extraordinary. During the late Ming period, eight friends from Wucheng practiced the *Śūramgama-sūtra* together, inviting [the Master] daily...
The spirit-medium discussed his arts with them until he died. Then another immortal arrived; the accounts he gave differed from those of the previous immortals.

Consequently, [the medium] served him with great intimacy for some time. Suddenly, he urged him to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name. When the others asked if reciting the Buddha’s name was permissible, he replied, "It is excellent."
The assembly all cried out, “Namo Buddha,” but [the Master] said, “It is not by such thoughts as these that one should practice. The assembly asked, “How then?
He replied, “You must join your palms with a sincere mind, prostrate toward the west, and recite ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha. The assembly followed his instructions.

Thereupon, he gave them a subtle and detailed exposition of the Dharma-gate of Mindfulness of the Buddha, leading them to abandon the false and return to the true, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Thus did he begin his teaching.
He revealed their past karmic connections, the names of the Bodhisattvas, and manifested various auspicious omens such as extraordinary fragrances and heavenly flowers.
Consequently, the eight individuals all turned away from their heterodox practices and returned to right faith. Wuxiu was the teacher among these eight;
the Bodhisattva sent him to the place of his preceptor Samadhi to receive the Vinaya and the complete monastic marks. At first, the preceptor hesitated.

Shortly thereafter, he encountered the Bodhisattva Yueji (Moon Verse). He then paid homage to the West and received tonsure from him. When the Bodhisattva first arrived, the assembly took him for an immortal;
they pointed to the moon as a subject and requested a verse. In response, the Bodhisattva showed them this verse: "The light of a single moon contains a thousand worlds;
Its manifestations are infinite, illuminating the delusions of the multitudes. One should know that its fundamental substance is originally non-dual. He did not... [text ends]

The mechanism for manifesting majestic transformations was set in motion beginning on the twenty-eighth day of the fifth month of the *jiwei* year of the Ming Chongzhen era, and concluding on the second day of the tenth month of the *dinghai* year of the Qing Shunzhi era. Over this period, there were twenty-four assemblies in total.

All that was taught therein concerns the essential subtleties of spiritual practice; because the verses contained phrases that precisely pointed out the path of authentic cultivation, it was subsequently titled *Xi*.
[The Master] pointed it out with certainty. As I read it, my body and mind leaped with joy, as if the finest *amṛta* (clarified butter) had dripped into my parched intestines.
I sighed in wonder without ceasing. The Monk said: "At first, I too did not believe it; however, upon reading it, my spirit was suddenly revitalized, and I could no longer disbelieve it.
I replied: "In former times, during the causal stage of his practice, the Bodhisattva [bestowed] upon the eight..."
Human beings possess great affinity; because their compassionate concern is profound, they are skillfully guided and led. How could this possibly be the same as the class of spirit-mediums?
Furthermore, observe that when the Bodhisattva was about to depart, he remarked: "The establishment of spirit-writing (luan-xi) is originally for spirits and ghosts to rely upon;
it is not something we can do anything about. This book was obtained from my friend Wang Guansan. It previously had woodblocks, which were recently destroyed.
Regarding this work by Huo, our fellow worthies intend to carve it once more for circulation in the world. I have carefully revised its chapters and sentences and arranged their sequence.
Having completed this, I have composed the preface as follows.
Autumn, the eighth month of the thirty-eighth year of the Qianlong era. Written by Peng Shaosheng, a junior disciple of Donglin, as the postscript to *The Certain Pointer to the Western [Paradise]*.
The ancient sages of the past are distant from us today; yet, by reading their books and understanding their words, one knows that they can certainly not be forged.

As for those who act, they simply sever [delusion] through principle. For fifteen hundred years since the Buddha-dharma entered China, there have been many heroic and sagely men among whom, upon encountering a single sutra or a single verse, attained decisive faith and entry, thereby liberating themselves from birth and death.

It is almost impossible to enumerate them all. Yet those of shallow intellect, relying on their private prejudices, speculate that its origins lie with Laozi and Zhuangzi, claiming it was forged by their followers.

However, since the texts of Laozi and Zhuangzi are still extant today, one need only take them and compare them with sutras such as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and the *Awakening of Faith* (*Yuanjue jing*) to see, at least in broad outline, the reasons for their differences in depth and their points of convergence or divergence. Lao...
If even Zhuangzi could not do it, how can one claim that those who study Laozi and Zhuangzi can?
This is the fault of those who fail to examine the underlying principles and instead follow their own private interests. In recent times, the practice of spirit-summoning (feiluan) has spread;

the sages and worthies of the Three Teachings have often responded to circumstances and inspired beings according to their capacities, propagating the Dharma and saving humanity—all of which arose from a heart of necessity. Upon reading this...
As for that book, knowing its script and understanding its words, one can decisively conclude that it cannot be a forgery; this is determined simply by reason. Its Western provenance is certain:
it is the Dharma taught by the Bodhisattva Jue-ming-miao-xing (Awakened, Luminous, and Wondrous Conduct) within the realm of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
As a teaching, it denounces deviant practices and points the way back to the Pure Land; it elucidates the wondrous truth of the single mind and exhausts the ultimate upward path.
[The Eight-Threaded] Barrier. This is truly a guide for those who study the Buddha’s teachings. I read it repeatedly and, sighing, exclaimed: "Alas!

The Land of Lotus Flowers is not separate from this very place; Amitābha Buddha is the total embodiment of all sentient beings. Yet, how is it that these beings do not realize this in their daily lives?
Never having given rise to a single thought of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), they enter deeper into delusion from one confusion to the next, drifting along for a long time."
How lamentable this kalpa is! The Bodhisattva’s vow of compassion is profound and heavy; he follows these sentient beings from lifetime to lifetime, never parting from them.
How does this transformation as a flying phoenix differ from manifesting a body to preach the Dharma?

Those who read this book, if they can truly believe in their own fundamental mind, practice according to the teaching, dedicate every thought toward awakening, remain free from all divergent thoughts, and reach a state where the mind is ultimate and emotions are empty—[then they shall attain liberation].
Suddenly liberated and dwelling nowhere, though one currently resides in this world of five turbidities, one’s entire being is already seated within the Land of Lotus Flowers.
When the conditions of this retribution-life are exhausted, rebirth occurs in the snap of a finger. Thus, the fruit and the cause are fundamentally without sequence.
If you do not believe in your own mind, you will consequently not believe in the Pure Land; worse yet, some may even suspect this book to be a forgery. If that is so, then for me, it is all over.
This book is the constant activity of the Great Bodhisattva’s emanations; how could it be regarded as mere spirit-writing?

At that time, I wished to have it carved for publication and widely circulated to benefit all sentient beings, yet the conditions were not yet harmonious. Until now, the spring of the Yiyou year (1945), [the opportunity has finally arrived].
Among the monastics, laypeople, and fellow practitioners on the path, there were none who did not rejoice and vow to provide financial support for its completion.

Some went so far as to weep while reading it, and read while weeping; they suddenly renounced their beloved dwellings, clothing, and utensils to enter the deep mountains to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha.
Is this not the inconceivable power of the Bodhisattva’s unconditioned compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*) in gathering and transforming sentient beings? Thereupon, [he] joined with Lingxi...
The two masters, Huiji and [the second master’s name], planned to have this work carved into printing blocks. Once the carving was completed, its beginning and end were thus recorded.
Written on the full moon of the ninth month in the Jiyou year of the Kangxi era by Langxi Jin E, a disciple of the Pure Land school from Gusu (Suzhou).
The Western Region specifically refers to the Bodhisattva Jue-ming-miao-xing (Awakened-Bright-Miraculous-Practice), who preached the Bodhisattva Precepts to his disciple Chang Sheji.
At one time, this Bodhisattva came from the Land of Ultimate Bliss and descended upon the ancient land of Gouwu in Zhendan (China). He was there...

He addressed his disciples: "By virtue of past causes and conditions, you have been able to receive my transformative guidance. Now, as the Bodhisattva is about to reveal the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, he spoke in verse:
The essential Dharma of all Buddhas Is subtle, secret, and inconceivable; Because it is beyond the reach of thought."
The Great Compassionate Father, the Muni, cannot be fully described; he speaks that which others cannot speak out of pity for sentient beings.
He guides them through future lives and further reveals blissful lands through diverse skillful means, causing them to resolve to be reborn there and thereby cross directly over all evil realms.
By virtue of the Buddha Amitābha’s great vows encompassing all beings, those who hear his name and are able to uphold it will certainly be born [in his land] without doubt.

If there are persons of great strength who single-mindedly recite [his name] with constant focus, they will achieve profound samādhi and see the Buddha before their very eyes; now I shall act according to the Buddha’s teaching.
I shall now open the gate of transformation and guidance; considering how you are deluded and inverted, I shall clearly point out the path of correct cultivation.

Regarding right and wrong and the strength or weakness of conditions, one should conceive the thought that [the Dharma] is difficult to encounter. Though the journey to the West spans ten billion leagues, a single moment of faith is sufficient.

After the Bodhisattva had spoken these verses, he had his disciples recite them clearly once. He then said, "You have long studied the profound arts of our school, yet your minds were immersed in heterodox practices.
Because my compassionate concern for you is deep due to our past affinities, I have come here to transform and guide you.
Now I have first established the Western Pure Land as the single gate of correct orientation and correct practice; yet I still fear that you may not yet possess ultimate faith."
Next, I shall speak of my name and what I have realized, so that you may know that the one who preaches this Dharma is a Great Bodhisattva.
Good son, in the past, while still on the path of causes, I used my wondrously profound awakened mind to illuminate all lands and everything possessed by sentient beings.
By means of the awakening to the wondrous and the wondrously awakened, and the luminous clarity of the wondrous mind, I gave rise to the immeasurable...
"Wonderful Practice! You shall deliver all sentient beings; therefore, Amitābha Buddha has sealed my name, calling me 'Awakened, Luminous, and of Wonderful Practice.

You all should take refuge in this from now on, without further doubt or duality. At that time, eight people in the assembly all joined their palms with single-minded devotion and recited "Namo Jue-ming-miao-xing Pusa" (Homage to the Bodhisattva Awakened, Luminous, and of Wonderful Practice). Having paid their respects, they rose. The Bodhisattva said, "Excellent!"
Indeed! It is thus.
Someone asked about the method for upholding dharanis and sutras. The Bodhisattva said: "What is called 'upholding dharanis and sutras' is simply upholding one's own mind.

The essential point lies in directly illuminating the ground of the mind (cittabhūmi). If one merely speaks of becoming proficient in upholding them, reciting them many times, or thinking of a particular sutra,"
One recites a mantra for a certain Buddha, claiming to possess great merit; yet one cannot dissolve each phrase back into one's own nature, nor can one deeply understand the Tathāgata’s subtle truth.
Claiming that one may thereby attain the fruit of realization, one does not see the crossroads.
Whether lacking eyes, or lacking feet, or being a begging woman, or a begging man, one never ceases throughout the day from chanting until the end.
At night, calculating what they have maintained, it amounts to no fewer than several hundred thousand recitations in a single year.
Yet, in the end, those who are disabled and those who beg for alms have never realized even a hair’s breadth of fruit. Why is this? It is simply because they lack both understanding and practice.
Therefore, one should know that to uphold this sutra, one must practice in accordance with this sutra and further make great vows. Or...
Whether seeking rebirth in the Buddha-land, seeking enlightenment of the mind-ground, generating great wisdom, or benefiting and saving sentient beings—
all rely upon the vast and far-reaching power of the Tathāgata’s propagation to fulfill the practitioner's vows. Only in this way does one truly uphold the sutras,
recite mantras, and practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
The Natural Old Monk, having suffered from a chronic illness that would not heal, wished to go to Mount Jing to await his death and have his remains interred in a communal stupa.
The Bodhisattva said, "If you wish to stay on the mountain to await death, you are merely seeking trouble where there is none.
Do you worry about where these few old bones will find a place to rest? You do not realize that when the light of the eyes falls to the ground, one simply stretches out both legs and lets it be."
Whether hacked by sword or axe, burned by fire, or submerged in water—it has nothing to do with you. To make long-term plans for the sake of others is also utterly foolish.
Furthermore, this body is of no benefit even while it is alive, let alone after death.
You should now simplify all affairs and single-mindedly hold to the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha," never abandoning it from moment to moment. Then Amitābha Buddha will—
I shall be your good companion; when the time of your great destiny arrives, I will manifest myself to guide you, so that you may be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Would this not be far better than entering the mountains to await death? Furthermore, birth, old age, sickness, and death are sufferings that cannot be avoided in this world.
Even though you have been ill for a long time, do not worry about whether you will recover or not; simply maintain a single thought and a single mind. Whether you live or die is up to others.
The other monk understood immediately.

When Sengbu'er went to the master to receive the precepts, the Bodhisattva said, "Alas, alas! With such a dignified countenance and such a prominent physical form, you do not know how to reflect upon yourself.
Judging by your actions, they are no different from those of a layperson. I see only your body..."
In this very place, one may wander through the hells. You must urgently and earnestly cultivate self-reflection, severing evil and following good;

seek the fruit of Buddhahood above and transform all sentient beings below. You must not remain in a state of dull ignorance, wasting this limited span of time and bringing upon yourself the burden of ten thousand kalpas.
Regarding the matter of receiving the precepts: it is better not to receive them at all than to receive them once and then fail to maintain them.
One must guard against even the slightest transgression, maintaining purity as flawlessly as a white jade disk or a bright pearl; only thus is the category of precepts fulfilled.
Indeed, the precepts are the very foundation for the Buddhas of the three periods of time to enter the Path; do not treat them with the levity of a child’s play.

Furthermore, whether dwelling in seclusion or traveling to study under various masters, one should further draw near to virtuous friends and distance oneself from those who are mediocre or inferior. By associating with the virtuous, the work of the Path will easily be accomplished.
"To associate with the wicked makes the observance of precepts easily lost. These two phrases are the essentials for studying the Way throughout one's entire life;

be careful and remember them. Ma Yongxi and his brothers were hunters in their previous lives. One day they entered the mountains and together killed a deer, for which they were to receive the retribution of a short lifespan.
Furthermore, they once saw a Buddha image in a stupa that had fallen to the ground; they helped it up, set it back in its seat, prostrated themselves, and departed.

Because of these wholesome causes, he again obtained a human body. After the Bodhisattva had first bestowed upon Yongxi an exposition [of the Dharma], Yongxi feared that his life would end and sought the Way of eternal longevity.
The Bodhisattva said: "In the past, at Miaojue Temple in the north, there was a novice śrāmaṇera who was sixteen years old.
At that time, a physiognomist who spoke of people’s births and deaths with an accuracy not off by even a hair’s breadth said to the śrāmaṇera: 'You..."
In the eighth month of autumn, at the age of eighteen, the śrāmaṇera was terrified that he was due to die.

That night, he prayed to the Buddha, wishing for a single scroll of scripture from the Tripitaka to be granted to him, so that he might uphold it for the rest of his life and pray for longevity. Having spoken these words, he wept uncontrollably;
after prostrating twice and rising, he reached into the Great Canon and, by chance, obtained the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He then transcribed it and began to uphold it. At dawn—
He was untiring by night. Furthermore, he maintained the precepts with rigorous discipline and fully realized the profound principles.

Before the age of forty, his reputation for the Way had spread far and wide, and the fourfold assembly looked up to him in devotion. He later passed away while seated at the age of eighty; he was the Venerable Weixing of Luoyang.

These events occurred during the sixth year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, which I personally witnessed. Since you are now terrified of a short lifespan and wish to seek longevity...

My son, you should rely upon this śrāmaṇera to seek the excellent root of the Vajra, resolve to write it down, diligently practice its recitation, and further seek to understand its meaning and intent;
these are internal merits. From this day forward, you must no longer kill living beings, but cherish them as you would yourself, and extensively accumulate hidden virtues;
these are external merits. By cultivating both internal and external merits together, [you shall attain success].
It is most great. When one can naturally become one in essence with Heaven, the principle that "heavenly longevity is not dual" is established.
Why worry that one’s years will not be long? Nevertheless, one must be as careful at the end as at the beginning, just like that śrāmaṇera who was eighty years old yet remained untiring.
Only then will you be in accord with the Way. Do not act so as to have a beginning but no end; do not practice for ten days or half a month, or even for a year or two, and then abandon it.

If you truly follow this throughout your entire life without interruption from beginning to end, and yet your aspirations are not fulfilled, then all the Buddhas and I alike shall fall into falsehood.
The Bodhisattva pointed to Chen Duanshu and said, "That you, father and son, have undertaken to practice my teaching is most rare and difficult to find.
However, you must maintain your resolve for a long duration; you must not give rise to thoughts of seeking immediate spiritual responses or signs of efficacy.
Only when you treat the two characters 'cultivation' (xiūxíng) as being like the matters of eating and wearing clothes in your daily life can you truly succeed."
The Bodhisattva showed the nun Chading Hongmu and said to her: "It is deeply pitiable that you have long harbored the aspiration for the Way yet have not encountered a true teacher.
Now, I shall provide you with a detailed exposition. In the past, when you were a bhikṣuṇī, you practiced with diligent vigor, never flagging day or night.
Because your mind was so intense, a certain vision suddenly arose within your state of meditative concentration, which said:"
"Why is it that I cannot quickly attain Buddhahood? On another day, he heard the words of the Buddhas regarding the signlessness of all phenomena and that "the mind itself is Buddha.
This further increased his heterodox thoughts, leading him to say: "Since all dharmas are empty and quiescent, and my own mind is Buddha, what need is there for cultivation?
He did not realize that this was the ultimate principle of emptiness, which is not easily expressed by those who have only recently entered the Dharma-realm. Thus he compared [himself] to them.
From this point on, Qiu fell completely into false views and ceased further cultivation. He claimed for himself that he had already realized the Great Way;

thus, he went from delusion into further delusion, sinking into the long night. How tragic it is for sentient beings who, seeking the Way, do not encounter a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and cannot avoid falling into the net.
You must be careful! You should now know that because of his past adherence to false views, this is his retribution.
Having incurred the five outflows and lost right mindfulness, you have further encountered false teachers; having been personally bitten by their poison, how could you not give rise to terror?
You should now swiftly arouse right faith and, with a sincere heart, mindfully recollect Amitābha Buddha, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The monk Wuxiu asked as a question, "How long is the span of one's life? The Bodhisattva showed him this verse:
Human life is like morning dew, Volatile and without fixed duration; Since one cannot yet escape dreams and illusions, Why must one seek to know it beforehand?

He further instructed him, saying: "For now, do not ask others about the date. When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, you will surely find yourself at a loss, with hands flailing and feet scrambling.
(It was on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month of the following year that Wuyouguo passed away from illness. Upon hearing this, Wuxiu requested further instruction. The Bodhisattva said:
"Yuanbo, you should know that to study the Way without clarifying this mind is like building a house without a foundation, or crossing water without a boat."
There is no raft. Those who wish to clarify the mind should minutely observe and investigate: from what do this body and this mind arise?

Since the four elements are empty and illusory, upon whom shall the mind rely? Once both body and mind are seen as illusions, there is no distinction whatsoever between them and the atoms of the world.
Regarding all phenomena at present: from where do they arise, and from where do they cease? If there is neither arising nor ceasing, then both the illumination and the illuminator have no basis.
Thus, one spontaneously beholds the ground of true suchness, the realm of quiescent extinction.
The scholar Kong of Gouqu had observed the fast for twenty years. Reflecting that he was now aged and infirm, he asked what would become of him after death;
thereupon, he wept incessantly. The Bodhisattva said, "There is no need for such grief and tears. Simply follow my words, believe them deeply, and practice accordingly;
you will naturally find a place of peace and security for yourself. He then bestowed upon him this verse:
In the West lies the Pure Land, upon which all humans and devas rely. You are able to cultivate this gate;
you shall be at peace, free from alarm or doubt.
Liu Wenzhou was renowned as a master of treating cold-induced illnesses (shanghan). Upon arriving, he paid his respects. The Bodhisattva asked him, "Has the cold entered your heart and pericardium?"
"What kind of illness should it be called? He replied, "It is named 'central cold' (zhōnghán). To illustrate this for you all, I say:
you know only that when cold enters the heart and the pericardium, it is called the disease of central cold; however, if evil [influences] enter the heart, it becomes a fatal illness."

All of you regard only physical illness as true illness; you regulate and treat it. Yet, when the mind suffers from a great illness, you do not consult a wise physician nor seek out marvelous medicine;
you simply endure the suffering of that affliction without realizing it. How lamentable!
Chen Daxin received instruction in the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) with the utmost sincerity. The Bodhisattva showed him this verse:
"The lotus has already been planted in the pond of eight virtues; Indeed, a single thought is most vast and profound.
Though its cultivation relies upon the power of the Tathāgata, Its growth depends entirely upon the resolute mind."
Furthermore, he said to the people by way of analogy: "In this land, there are those who make a vow to be reborn in that land; they shall immediately be born within lotus flowers there.
Therefore, you should give rise to deep faith."
Sun Zhongbai was fond of alchemy, yet after many days he had seen no results. He came to the assembly and paid his respects;
the Bodhisattva rebuked him, saying, "You old bald-pate, have you come to show me this face today? Let me ask you: when will your elixir of gold be perfected?"
The respondent said, "I shall seek to achieve it exactly as you say. The Bodhisattva said, "If you succeed in achieving it, leave aside several grains for me;
do not eat them all down into your belly. When you meet the Old Man Yama, you will need to perform some social courtesies to present to him.
You foolish old fellow, there is absolutely no share of this for you; it would be better to go about your own proper business. The monk bowed in thanks.
After a short while, the Bodhisattva spoke again: "Foolish old man, do you know your own original nature?
He replied, "I seek to see my nature; that is my original state. The Bodhisattva asked, "Do you know whether this nature is large or small, blue or yellow?
He replied, "Nature has no such characteristics. The Bodhisattva said, "If that is so, then where do you intend to go?"
He requested an audience. Sun remained silent. The man then sent a letter of faith in surrender, wishing to become a disciple and requesting that a dharma-name be bestowed upon him.
Sun thereupon granted him a verse, saying:
"In nature there are no distinctions of large or small, nor of blue or yellow; How could there be name or fame? Call it whatever you will."
If one does not penetrate the profound and subtle point herein, every single word and character will be muddled and erroneous.
I shall now forcefully establish a name for you: you may be called "One Who Has Reached the Source. From this time forward, you have no more than seven or eight years remaining.
Do not let the thirty-six years of ascetic practice from eight hundred years ago go to waste. Sun then asked about this.

"How does one reach the ultimate conclusion? the Bodhisattva replied, "To reach the conclusion is simply to reach the conclusion. He asked again, "How does one reach the conclusion? Sun then asked, "How should one practice?
The Bodhisattva said, "The single gate of the Pure Land can widely encompass all classes of beings. Regarding your question on practice:
you should contemplate Amitābha Buddha, make the vow to be reborn there, and thus achieve everything at once—this is 'one thing settled, and all things settled. You..."
There shall be no further delusion.
The Bodhisattva further addressed the people, saying: "From antiquity, the great sages and worthies have expounded the subtle and established the teachings; all were most refined and most concise.

Those of superior capacity attained awakening upon hearing them, while those of middling and inferior capacity cultivated themselves upon hearing them; all returned to the Great Way. Yet later generations produced..."

[The author] states: He busies himself with prolix and obscure discourse, causing ordinary people to speculate based on their preconceived notions. Consequently, errors are passed down as further errors, leading them deep into heterodoxy and depravity.

They die in the world clutching their ignorance, never realizing it themselves. For example, those who read texts such as the *Daben* (Reaching the Root), *Cantong* (Penetrating the Same), and *Wuzhen* (Awakening to Truth) do not understand the essential principles of the Dharma;
they blindly believe in erroneous traditions, claiming to have attained realization, and cling to these views with avarice, refusing to let go. [Thus ends the] White [Pleading].
Those whose minds are devoid of accomplishment and are stirred by various afflictions—the Bodhisattvas declare these to be truly pitiable.
Therefore, since you have recognized your former errors, you should now cultivate right faith.

At one time, as the Bodhisattva was about to arrive at the Dharma assembly, his eight disciples—Wuxiu, Changshe, Changyuan, Dingmao, Daben, Chadinghong, Chengdingduan, and Chadingmin—stood with reverent composure and waited expectantly, chanting the Buddha’s name in unison.
Suddenly, they smelled a wondrous fragrance wafting from the sky. The assembly was filled with joy, having experienced something unprecedented. The Bodhisattva said, “Excellent!”

"Excellent! Do you know whether there was a karmic affinity for this assembly today? Long ago, in the sixth year of the Tianjian era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, I left the household life at Jingyin Monastery in the eastern capital of Northern Wei as a great bhikṣu.
Fleeing the chaos, I traveled south and took up residence at the foot of Mount Jiming. At that time, you eight people relied upon me to study; before long, due to the military..."

The chaos dispersed. Two years after I had passed beyond [this life] at Tianzhu in Wulin, I was again born as the eldest son of Prince Xian of Qinghe during the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang dynasty;

I likewise renounced my station and left the household life. Now, that you eight people have gathered here together to recite the Buddha’s name is due to the resolve I first formed, no different from the past. It is only that since you departed from me...
It has been more than eight hundred years since then, yet you have continued to drift and wander without returning; this is truly pitiable and truly painful.
Now, for your sake, I shall further elucidate the practices you must cultivate so that they may be swiftly accomplished and you may quickly ascend to liberation.
You should each listen with careful attention.
He said to Wuxiu: "Although you have previously engaged in the profound gate, you have been able to show reverence toward the Buddhas;

know that this is indeed a karmic cause from former lives. Now you should swiftly give rise to the profound mind and diligently cultivate pure deeds to serve as a guide for all people, lest your efforts be cast away in vain.
This was the thirteenth year [of his life]. He entrusted him with these verses:"
Eight hundred years ago there was a superior affinity; meeting now, we point to the blue sky.
One already knows the mid-autumn moon of one’s own original ground; do not seek a ferryboat upon the long river. Shishi said to Changshe:
"You constantly maintain the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī. How do you maintain it? He replied: "That which is maintained..."
The mantra is distinct and clear; yet the mind that can maintain it is utterly unattainable. The Bodhisattva said:
"To maintain it in this manner is called true maintenance. I have a verse to entrust to you."
"You who uphold the Great Compassion Mantra should recognize the mind of great compassion; being free from both name and form, you shall thereby deliver all living beings.

He then showed the source of permanence, saying: "Now that you have left the household life, you must be humble and gentle, serving your teachers and elders with reverence, and emptying yourself [of pride]."
He requested further instruction to increase his resolve, saying, "Do not merely spend your days sitting amidst clouds and mist;
you have not yet reached the source. He showed him again, saying, "You are so utterly bewildered—can you understand your own mind?
Yuan remained silent. The Master then ordered him to recite the Cundī Dhāraṇī once. As Yuan recited it accordingly, the Bodhisattva asked, "This is not your mind. What do you call it?"
The verse says:
When you perceive the initial absence of mind, That is your own fundamental mind. Recite the Cundī mantra once;
The entire body will be clearly revealed. Ding Mao said: "As you maintain the Cundī mantra, you must always apply yourself with subtle and meticulous mindfulness. Observe all..."
Whether the environment be noisy or tranquil, whether it be material objects or non-material, whether there be joy or weariness—none of these are not the manifest essence of this mantra;
they are my wondrous mind flowing forth at every moment. If you uphold it in this manner, you will certainly attain the fruit of realization.
I shall also assist you in your accomplishment through my spiritual power. You should recite this verse of mine:

The two lines of secret teaching are your own original mind. Do not say that the Dharma is meager; this Dharma is profoundly deep. He asked Da-ben, "How will you proceed? He replied, "I wish to clarify the mind.

The Bodhisattva said, "Have you not fallen into mere lip service? You should diligently practice mindfulness of the Buddha; its merit will be tenfold. He also showed him a verse: The two lines of secret teaching are your own original mind. Do not say that the Dharma is meager; this Dharma is profoundly deep.
If you wish to clarify the mind, do not rely on words alone. Diligently practice mindfulness of the Buddha; its merit is tenfold.
Outside the mind there is no Buddha; the Buddha is your own mind. With deep faith and without doubt, realize in a single thought that there is no arising. Shi Chading Hong said:
"When you uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, you should know there are seven ways it is not upheld: namely, it is not upheld when the mind is dull or distracted;
it is not upheld when there are transgressions or offenses; it is not upheld after entering an impure place; and it is not upheld after drinking alcohol."
One maintains it. If one is distracted by people and lacks purity, one does not maintain it. If there are pending affairs, whether already underway or yet to be done, one does not maintain it.
If the mind is preoccupied with other memories, one does not maintain it. If one intends to uphold it with a firm resolve, one should distance oneself from these seven [conditions].

Once the recitation has become proficient, one should maintain it within the state of meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*). If one can indeed do so, then the merit will be inconceivable and the karmic fruition will be inconceivable.
The Buddha has given a sincere word: "You must take responsibility for this. Furthermore, I give you this verse:
The single scripture of Prajñāpāramitā Has inexhaustible merit; It uproots the root of deluded thoughts And liberates one from the disease of birth and death.
[He] showed Chen Dingduen, saying: "When petty men do evil, they only fear that others will know of it. When gentlemen do good..."
Furthermore, he was also constantly fearful that others might know [of his practice]. You should perform Buddhist services with the mind of a gentleman who is cautious regarding the Way.
Moreover, there is a verse that says:
Do not prize being known by others; Do not hope for divine responses. Always unify your mind; It must be firm and upright.
He said to Cha Ding-min, "That you, not yet having reached the age of twenty, already know how to turn toward the Way, serves as proof of your past causes.
I shall now name you Min. 'Min' (敏) carries four meanings: intelligence, diligence, subtlety, and agility. Intelligence is to remove your darkness;
diligence is to encourage your laziness; subtlety is to open your wisdom; and agility is to stimulate your stagnation. You should reflect upon the name and contemplate its meaning; do not..."
The Bodhisattva said, "I have merely given you this one word. I shall further show you a verse: 'Your years are still young;
you should study filial piety and fraternal duty. By means of this, sustain yourself; do not let your will become indolent.
On that day, Chen Daxin arrived later. The Bodhisattva asked, "How do you practice and maintain yourself? He replied, "I simply practice..."
"Pure Land. The Bodhisattva said: "Apart from this, there is no other superior gateway. I entrust to you one verse: 'The Way has no other teaching; it is mind-only.
When the lotus womb is first formed, apply yourself with single-minded devotion and do not be dualistic.
The Bodhisattva said: 'The Pure Land gateway you have shown is truly the heart-essence of all Buddhas and the direct path for humans and devas. Now, you—
Although others may seek rebirth in that land, if their aspiration is not earnest, it will be like entering the sea without obtaining a precious jewel;
it will be a mere labor with no benefit. In the past, during the time of Emperor Ming of the Jin dynasty, I received the body of a poor man.
Because of my poverty and suffering, I made a great vow, saying: "Due to my past karma, I have received this bitter retribution. If today I am unable to see Amitābha..."
"Amitābha Buddha! May I be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and achieve all merits. Even at the cost of losing my life, I shall never retreat from this vow.
Having made this oath, he focused his mind with single-minded diligence for seven days and seven nights.

Thereupon, his mind was opened, and he beheld the marks and signs of Amitābha Buddha’s radiant glory pervading the worlds of the ten directions. Before the Buddha, I personally received the prediction of my future enlightenment; subsequently, after seven...

At fifteen, he passed away while seated and was reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Later, due to the weight of his vows to deliver sentient beings, he returned to this world to manifest his transformative influence according to circumstances.
Sometimes he appeared as a bhikṣu, sometimes as a layperson, sometimes as a king, sometimes as a minister, sometimes as a woman, and sometimes as a butcher or a beggar.
Whether hidden or manifest, whether acting in accordance with or contrary to worldly ways, he always taught the Dharma in accordance with the needs of those he encountered.

I guide all classes of beings. Furthermore, because those on the path of the immortals (*ṛṣi*) have for the most part not yet awakened to the true permanence, they indulge in the pleasure of long life and do not contemplate further cultivation.
I manifest the body of an immortal to rescue them from their deluded fall, as in the case of one individual during the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang dynasty.
Now, I shall again clarify the heterodox and the orthodox for you all and proclaim the Pure Land. You should all focus your intent and unify your minds, cultivating with steadfast resolve.
This gateway is certainly not deceptive. If one’s resolve is singularly firm, one need not wait for a future life to be born [in that realm];
even in the present life, one may behold the Buddha, no different from my own experience in years past. There is a four-line verse:
Speak but a single word; recite the Buddha’s name but once. If you can bring the thought-moment to death, I grant that your Dharma-body shall live.
Someone asked: "How may a student leave behind worldly desires and attain freedom from hindrances? The Bodhisattva said: "I shall lead you by way of..."
"Extrapolate from the small to the great; extrapolate from the external to the internal. You all should understand this meaning well.
Suppose someone here were to take a single coin from you without cause—would you feel anger? They replied: 'Though a single coin is insignificant, we would feel anger if it were taken.
Again, suppose someone were to give you a single coin without cause—would you feel joy? They replied: 'Though a single coin is insignificant...'"

When they saw that he was giving, they were pleased. One replied, "A single coin is extremely insignificant; why is it worth being joyful about? Another said, "There is nothing to be angry about in taking [it away].
The Bodhisattva said, "If you can act in this way, your mind has been pure for a long time. Why is it still submerged in turbidity and defilement today?
You should know that when practitioners do not purify their minds with diligence, whether they perceive things as existing or non-existing, they are attached in every instance."
Every thought-moment is characterized by greed; thus, the karmic consciousness rushes about in confusion, never stopping for even a moment.
Even when you recite the single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha," your mental focus still wanders outward, unable to return to a single point for even an instant.

This is truly because, throughout immeasurable kalpas, you have never once given rise to the mind that seeks to distance itself from worldly desires for even a single hour or day. Therefore, these worldly desires—
Since beginningless kalpas, it has never for even a single moment or day been willing to depart from your mind.
Your body is entangled and your mind is bound, deeply immersed in the net of worldly dust; how then could you be like a lotus flower that emerges from the mud yet remains unstained?

Therefore, know that if you wish to sever greedy attachment, you must first practice the contemplation of relinquishment regarding the taking and giving of even a single coin. By cultivating the contemplation that "this is not mine," the act of seizing will not arise.
Anger is that which gives rise to a lack of joy. This applies in the same way to everything from hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions of coins up to billions of coins;
from kingdoms, cities, wives, and children, up to one’s own body, flesh, marrow, and bones;

from the mind, thought, and consciousness of the past, present, and future, up to birth and death, karmic retribution, bodhi, and nirvana—all are exactly like this. It is the same as with a single coin.

There is no difference in their eradication. Spontaneously, habitual outflows are extinguished; obstructive conditions are forever ceased. One gradually treads upon purity and accomplishes the factors of enlightenment.
You all should practice in accordance with this; do not again harbor doubts regarding obstacles.
On the second day of the first month of winter, the anniversary of the Bodhisattva’s birth, the assembly prepared offerings and celebrated his longevity.

The Bodhisattva asked, "With what do you wish to offer me long life? They all replied, "We take our hearts as our offering. The Bodhisattva asked, "What is this 'heart' that can be used as an offering?
They answered, "It is simply ultimate sincerity; its very nature is without substance. The Bodhisattva said, "If it is said to be without substance,"
"Who knows that ultimate sincerity? One who can know sincerity must certainly have a location where it may be pointed out.

How can it be said there is no such thing? He replied, "In truth, nothing is obtained. The Bodhisattva asked, "When you say 'nothing is obtained,' do you mean it is temporarily non-existent, or is it definitively non-existent?

While the assembly deliberated but had not yet responded, the Bodhisattva said, "If it is non-existent, it is definitively non-existent; if it exists, it is definitively existent. One [or the other]."
When one delves into subtle doubts, a difference of a hair’s breadth leads to a distance of a thousand li.

You should know that whether your words are sincere or false, whether you speak of the Way as existing or non-existing, all are merely the workings of a mind that calculates, scrutinizes, and speculates through arising and ceasing. To offer such things as prayers to me will be of no benefit whatsoever.
Listen instead to my wondrous verse.
The Ultimate Truth has no dualistic mind; the Ultimate Truth has immeasurable mind. Mind is not any mind, and all natures are not mind.
By eliminating the unreal deluded mind, one relies on the true mind, which is merely given the provisional name "true";
thus, both "true" and "deluded" are not established. Homage to the Honored Śākyamuni! One realizes that the mind has no location.

While he was using skillful means to bring merit to all living beings, his disciples all bowed twice and wished to hear further the essentials of the Dharma. The Bodhisattva said, "Excellent, excellent!
Since you wish to hear further the essentials of the Dharma, you should understand my words with sincerity and answer my questions well. O disciples, it is like this:
Someone said to another person, "The capital of the Emperor in Yanjing is incomparably wealthy and noble. Upon hearing these words, did that person have the ambition to go there?
They all replied, "We wish to go. The Bodhisattva asked, "You do not know the way; how will you proceed?
They all replied, "There are people who can point it out; we shall follow their directions. The Bodhisattva said, "That will not do. Suppose those people were to point you in the wrong direction..."
[The direction] faces south toward the east. If one does not discern this clearly and instead follows their words, then the capital of Yan will be further and further away.
The assembly asked, "If that is so, what should be done? The Bodhisattva said, "Ultimately, find a person who has traveled past the capital of Yan and instruct this person, saying:
'You must travel toward the north; then you shall reach the presence of the Emperor directly. O disciples, as for this person..."

"Is there any error in this? They all bowed their heads and said, "There is no error. The Bodhisattva said, "Furthermore, suppose there is a person who wishes to ascend to the summit of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff or the top of a nine-story tower. How should one instruct them? They all replied, "From the low to the high."
The Bodhisattva said: "Indeed, it has been said of old: 'A journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet.
One must proceed from the first step to the second, and so on until reaching the highest step; only then can it be called the correct teaching.
To say that one takes a single step and immediately leaps to the highest point is mere idle talk. Furthermore, it is like a person to whom a Son of Heaven issues a mandate to appoint them to office."
That person asked, "Do you wish to be a prime minister or a minor official? How did those people answer? They all said, "We certainly wish to be prime ministers.
The Bodhisattva said, "Indeed. Furthermore, it is like a person standing at a fork in the road who does not know which way to go;
someone feeling pity for him points and says, "This side is extremely perilous and full of sharp turns; one cannot emerge from it easily."
"The head. This side is extremely straight and large; it is extremely level. If one walks along it, one will emerge with the head.
The man followed the instruction and asked, "Between these two sides, which path should I take? They all replied, "Walk the straight one; walk the level one. The Bodhisattva said, "Excellent."
"Excellent! Your responses to my questions are all in accord with correct principle. However, are you able to clearly understand my parable?
They all bowed again and said, "Please grant us your instruction. The Bodhisattva said, "Listen well.
Although you have long possessed the aspiration for the Way, you do not recognize the essentials of its cultivation; your progress lacks a foundation. It is like a person who wishes to travel..."

This is like being in the capital city of Yan but not knowing the way there. If one encounters a false teacher who instructs one in a false dharma, it is as if the capital were in the north, yet one is instead pointed toward the east or the south.
In such a case, even if that person travels all day long, they will remain lost without a destination;
how could they possibly have an audience with the Supreme Honored One? How could they possibly realize the Great Way? Now, the Amitābha whom I point out—
The Pure Land is the imperial capital. Through the three—faith, vow, and practice—if one applies oneself with diligent perseverance, one will ultimately attain rebirth there;
this is the progression from the first stage to the highest stage. To aspire to the highest grade (Jōhon) is like wishing to become a high minister rather than a minor official.
To cultivate according to this is to walk the straight path and not follow crooked ways. I shall now proceed along it.
You are people who have passed beyond the capital city of Yan. If you cannot place deep faith in this, it is as if you were abandoning the imperial capital to hasten toward the frontier lands;
forsaking the dignity of a prime minister to descend to the meanness of a minor official; turning one's back on the upright and great to seek out the difficult and obscure.
The peaks of ten-thousand-fathom mountains and the summits of nine-storied pagodas are not within your reach—how truly lamentable!
"How painful it is!

You all wish to accumulate fields as a means for your practice. The Bodhisattva said, "If you wish to vow to study together, gathering for a long time without dispersing, and severing ties with worldly affairs, such that you no longer need to devise plans to seek food and clothing from others, then you may do so. Thus he spoke these words.
Consider this: as I see it, although your intention is good, it ultimately remains an attachment to worldly toil and is not the pure Dharma.
Why is this? Taking a single meal on the street and spending a single night at a burial mound were the models of the former Buddhas.
If you must rely upon cultivated fields to practice, should you fail to obtain even one, then none of you would ever have a day for cultivation. Furthermore, if you say...
To lack the necessary funds and attempt to raise them through public solicitation is likewise unacceptable. Throughout the Buddha’s lifetime of teaching, these two words do not exist.
They are merely the actions of those in the degenerate age who fail to recognize propriety and righteousness, who fear neither cause and effect nor shame.
A true practitioner of the Way, for whom the thought of birth and death is urgent, will certainly never entertain such an intention. However, there is one further point to be made.
All of you, simply maintain right mindfulness and each exert yourselves. This is precisely gathering without gathering.

If body and mind are dissipated, affairs will lack constancy; this is gathering in appearance but actually being scattered. If you clearly understand this meaning, you should simply act according to your capacity and the occasion;
do not engage in idle reflections or premature planning.
The Bodhisattva further addressed the assembly, saying: "Do you all worry that your bodies are entangled in the worldly net, such that your thoughts cannot be purified?
I have a method for you: simply give rise to the vow to distance yourselves from this world and seek deliverance;

by resolutely turning toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss with a heart that beholds Amitābha Buddha, you can exchange your mind of rushing after profit and fame for this [new resolve], and thus be able to..."
One awakens upon the very path of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). Someone asked:
"If one is unable to achieve single-mindedness in the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), what skillful means (*upāya*) should be employed? The Bodhisattva replied:

"You need only cease fixed conceptualizations and recite slowly. You must ensure that the sound accords with the mind and the mind follows the sound. After a long period of such recitation, you will naturally attain it."
All his thoughts became clear and lucid; the mind and its objects were severed from all illumination, and he entered the *nien-fo samādhi*.
However, in ordinary life, one must recite the Buddha’s name many times—from a thousand to ten thousand—without interruption of the mind, for only then will the faculties most easily reach maturity.

If one forces the mind to be focused on a single point, it will ultimately not be so. At that time, Da Ben was at the Master’s side; suddenly, he startled and recited the name several times. The Bodhisattva said:

"So it is, so it is. Since you disciples have long accumulated sincerity in your desire to fashion images for veneration and have requested instruction on the characteristics of the Dharma, it is fitting that I reveal them to you.
Yet, while you dwell amidst the dust and toil of worldly afflictions, I abide within the wondrous clarity of the inner mind."
It is manifest right now, yet you are unable to see it. Furthermore, as I transform beings according to their individual capacities, my physical manifestations are not uniform.
For now, however, following the practice that arises from the fundamental source, you may depict me in the form of a great bhikṣu, with a face like the full moon and a body of majestic proportions.
He wears the kashaya robe and sits upon a lotus flower; his left hand rests on his knee, while his right hand performs the gesture of preaching the Dharma. Between his eyebrows...
He emitted white light from his ūrṇā-kośa. Within the light was Amitābha Buddha, seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

His marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) had to be strictly adorned; they must not be rendered in a careless or hasty manner. Having heard this, everyone stood with palms joined in reverence and contemplated such dharmic characteristics.
The Bodhisattva then said: "Disciples, each person possesses a wondrous practice of awakening and clarity. It is neither identical to nor separate from you."
Where people search but do not find, it appears from time to time, being manifest and clear even now; there is no further need to fashion images or offer worship—may you behold it on another day.
Chadinhong, having lost his son, wished to renounce his home and become a monk. The Bodhisattva said, "Do not harbor such deluded thoughts for now; this matter is not something you can accomplish.
You should simply rectify your mind to govern your mind, and rectify your body to govern your body. Sever all unbeneficial activities and distance yourself from all unbeneficial friends.
Turn your heart toward the Great Awakened One and vow to emerge from the path of delusion. He then drew from that vast [ocean of wisdom].

"May it nourish my parched soil. I pray with earnestness for your empowerment to dispel all obstructive conditions. As you previously feared for your longevity and physical well-being, you should now direct your efforts toward this;
do not speak much more. Dinghong then asked: "I have received the instructions to uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
However, as there are differing versions of its various words and phrases, which text should I follow to ensure there is no error? The Bodhisattva said: "The *Vajra*..."
The seven characters of "Prajñāpāramitā" are entirely without error.
When Shen Tianshu fell ill, he made offerings and requested a prophecy. The Bodhisattva said, "As for your current illness, you shall not die just yet."
One should cease all entanglements and settle the mind in upright sitting. Contemplate the impermanence of the body; contemplate the impermanence of the world.
Let go of all false conditions entirely. Slowly recite the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha," and naturally the six sense-objects will not arise.
With a single-minded purity, this will not only heal the illness of your present life, but the very root of the disease of birth and death shall also be uprooted from it.

Your current request for instruction is merely a hope that I might have some excellent method or oral transmission to give you, which could cure your ailment; how could you know that Bodhisattvas possess no such deceptive methods? It is only this...

I have merely instructed you with these words of reality upon reality. If you believe and practice them, they are truly a single dose of the supreme elixir of the highest grade. I entrust this verse to you.
Illness arises from oneself; it is likewise removed by oneself. By purifying the mind through focused concentration, one attains constant peace and joy—steadfast, enduring, and unchanging.
Wumingiaoshou Bodhisattva said to Shida: "You have a profound aspiration to investigate and clarify the ground of the mind. However, you must first empty your mind."
"Leather, sand, lead, water, fire"—these and such talk as "the original face," "true emptiness," and "true purity" are, in fact, utterly obstructive.
How can you possibly practice with them? If you would truly practice, you must cast this entire bundle away into the great ocean of the Eastern Sea;
otherwise, you will labor in vain and waste your efforts. It is better to recite [the name] with absolute certainty.

A single utterance of "Amitābha Buddha": herein lies the clarification of the mind, and herein lies rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. To attain both at once with a single movement—this is the ultimate expediency.
Wu Xiu asked, "How does one honor and repay one's ancestors? The Bodhisattva replied, "Regarding what is called filial piety in the world, what is considered supreme?

He said, "Being able to provide respectful care, being able to perform good deeds, and not forgetting the virtues of one's predecessors. The Bodhisattva said, "While these constitute filial piety, they are limited.

Only by being able to give rise to great vows and cultivate the supramundane Dharma can one truly fulfill it. If one attains the Way and fulfills its fruition, how could this be merely a matter of worldly blessings?"

As well as the nine patriarchs—indeed, all those who have been enemies or kin throughout kalpas—shall together attain liberation. That you are able to single-mindedly cultivate the Pure Land is what constitutes great filial piety.
Dingmao asked: "How does the recitation of mantras clarify the mind? How does it lead to ultimate realization? The Bodhisattva replied: "The mind does not depart from the mantra."
The mantra does not depart from the mind; this is the meaning of "upholding. You should, at all times, contemplate whether the essence of this mantra and the essence of my own mind are one or two.
If you say they are two, how can the mind uphold the mantra, and how can the mantra manifest the mind?
If it is said that [the mantra] is one, why is it that when one forgets it, the mantra is absent, and when one remembers it, the mantra is present?

From this, one knows that this mantra and the mind are free from all names and characteristics; they are ultimately empty and quiescent. This is called the ultimate. If one merely recites it without reaching this ultimate, there will be no wondrous understanding.
How can the great wisdom of equality be manifested? If the great wisdom of equality does not appear, by what means could it be illuminated?
"Have you reached the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the three realms, which lies beyond the delusion of birth and death?

When you asked about reaching the source, you said that reciting the Buddha’s name aloud easily causes fire to flare up; may I recite it silently? The Bodhisattva said, "Whenever you recite the Buddha’s name once, you say that fire flares up.
Why is it that when you talk to people all day long, not even a trace of fire arises? You should know that this 'fire' is your own..."

For immeasurable kalpas, ignorance and afflictions have accumulated; because your faith today is not genuine, mindfulness arises following the fire, and the fire is produced by chasing after delusion, thereby burning away your Dharma-body and the life-force of wisdom.

In the past, for the sake of the Great Dharma, the World-Honored One, the Muni, sacrificed his body to seek the Way over immeasurable kalpas, which is why he was able to attain the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment].
O King of Jewels, now that your years and strength have already declined, you practice diligently from morning until night yet still lament that it is too late.
You remain attached to the toils of worldly existence, hoping for elixirs to seek longevity and increased life.

Have you not heard that even in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception there is an exhaustion of karmic retribution, where the kalpa-fire burns through everything down to the third dhyāna heaven? How much more so for these trivial, conditioned supports of water, fire, lead, and mercury?
How can one seek from the nature of conditioned phenomena that which is eternally free from change and extinction?

Now that you have heard my words, you should regard them as if awakening from a dream or sobering from intoxication; diligently cultivate the Pure Land and, with right mindfulness, attain rebirth there.
The lifespan in that world is infinite and inexhaustible; one achieves the Dharma-body and reaches all-knowledge—this is not a mere shallow longevity of long-lived observation.
These methods cannot be discussed as being on the same level.
When Cha Dinghong asked, "When reciting mantras, I often experience great fear; I beg for instruction on a skillful means," the Bodhisattva said: "Who comes to frighten you?
Who is it that experiences the fear? It is because your habitual tendencies from previous lives are impure that [fear arises] from within subtle thoughts."
"This manifestation has suddenly appeared; you need only recite and uphold [the mantra] with sincerity, and it shall naturally be extinguished.

You will attain your heart's desires, your intentions will be fulfilled, you will be well able to subdue and restrain the afflictions (*kleśa*), and you will enter the profound and subtle. What cause for fear is there?"
Chen Dingyu offered prayers for his mother’s illness, asking what meritorious deeds he should perform to ensure her complete recovery. The Bodhisattva showed him this verse:
Filial piety is the foremost of all virtues; Filial piety penetrates the three realms of existence. How great is the practice of filiality! It is the teacher of human relations.
With a sincere heart, you seek to cure your mother’s illness; you should remain at ease, yet constantly mindful of your mother’s suffering.
When you eat fine delicacies, think of how your mother has reduced her intake of food.
When you wear light and soft garments, think of how your mother’s chest and ribs are exposed, her clothes stained with pus and blood. Reflecting thus, you shall find no rest by day or night.
I take refuge in the Great Sage, whose sincerity is singular and unwavering, who diligently practices all manner of goodness, and who looks upward to repay the four debts of gratitude.
May your mother’s blessings increase; may her lifespan grow longer; may her illness be cured; and may her body be healthy and strong.
Bodhisattva Jue Ming, as your protector and refuge, if you act according to these words, there shall be no wish that is not fulfilled.
Dingmao wished to abandon the recitation of mantras and instead practice mindfulness of the Buddha, so he asked for instruction. The Bodhisattva said:

"If you wish to abandon the recitation of mantras and practice mindfulness of the Buddha with single-minded devotion, that is most excellent. However, you do not yet understand the essential points of the Dharma;

you may only be called a person who observes the fasts and loves goodness, but you cannot be called a person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha. Why is this? To cross the great ocean, one must be fully equipped..."

One who wishes to travel a thousand li in a great ship must first select a fine horse; likewise, a person who contemplates the Buddha (nienfo) must first possess great capability to sever all entanglements and tear open the net of dust.
Directly and immediately, that which is mindfulness is the Buddha, and that which is the Buddha is the mind.

Even to the point of transcending both "is" and "is not," one suddenly enters the Great Radiant Treasury (Mahā-prabhāsvara-kośa) of the Tathāgata. Only in this way is it called "right mindfulness of the Buddha."
One is named a person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha. You should understand this meaning well.
Then four young monks came forward to pay their respects. The Bodhisattva said, "Young men, since beginningless time, sentient beings..."

It is because of affection that one forms a family; yet within a family, parents are the most profound source of kindness toward their children and their love for them is most intimate, making it difficult to part with or abandon them.

Now that you have left the secular world to become bhikṣus, you must recognize that your parents owe you a debt of gratitude even greater than ordinary kindness—a kindness beyond the power of words to describe. Therefore, you should take advantage of this opportunity.

In this prime of youth and vigor, one must diligently cultivate the path; only by repaying one's parents with the sincere resolve to sever worldly ties and renounce affection can one truly be without shame regarding the two characters "renunciant.

If, however, one remains indolent and negligent, leading to a life spent in ruin and failure, this is the most unfilial of unfilial acts, making one the gravest sinner in all under heaven. You should, therefore, because of me—
Upon hearing these words, Mengsheng was struck with a sense of profound sorrow.
The Bodhisattva again addressed the assembly, saying: "Good sons, this human body is born of one's parents and nurtured by one's parents.
All the various endeavors and various enjoyments you currently experience—even if your parents were never..."
It is like gaining a single coin; yet it was your parents who gave birth to your body, making it possible for you to exist today. Among all matters, the body is the greatest;
the body is the foundation. If one traces back from this foundation, is it not the kindness of one's parents that is difficult to express and impossible to exhaust?
Therefore, the Buddha said: "If one utters a loud voice or speaks harshly toward one's parents, one still incurs immeasurable demerit; how much more so for those who act even more severely than this?
If one says that because the parents treat them with unbearable severity, one must not refrain from disputing with them, then one regards one's parents as mere strangers.
One should instead joyfully accept their treatment, for it is the parents' own [karmic lot]."
On the day of awakening, one must by no means contend over who is right and who is wrong, becoming a person who defies heaven and violates human ethics.
The Bodhisattva said: "Disciples, you should know that the Buddhas of the ten directions are the minds of sentient beings, and the sentient beings of the ten directions are the minds of the Buddhas.
Therefore, when you recollect the Buddha and think of the Buddha, the Buddhas of the ten directions will manifest within your own mind. Thus it is.
Nor do the Buddhas enter into your mind, nor does your mind emerge from the Buddhas;
all are the wondrous, fundamental luminosity of awakening, which is inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva said: "Where the movements of the mind cease, this is the eternally abiding true mind of all Buddhas;
where the movements of the mind exist, this is the karma-mind of birth and death for sentient beings. Between these two, there is not even room for a hair’s breadth.

If you can apply yourself with persistent and meticulous effort, ensuring that this mind is without even a fraction of a gap, only then will you attain some degree of resonance. Do not practice in a perfunctory manner for merely half a year or ten months."
One might then say, "I am able to practice the Way with great diligence," not realizing that this is precisely what constitutes an obstacle to the Way; one must be extremely careful regarding this.

Furthermore, although you may apply effort, if you have not yet reached the state where it is like a copper mountain or an iron wall—neither to be pushed down nor moved—you have not yet realized the attainment of a single integrated whole.
Do not, upon seeing some slight reflection or sign, immediately cease your efforts; this would constitute being halfway through the path.
To abandon it will inevitably lead to the loss of all prior effort, resulting in no benefit whatsoever. This, moreover, is a grave illness of those who study the Way, which one must recognize.
One must understand that the Buddha-dharma is like a great ocean; the further one enters, the deeper it becomes. It is by no means something that can be exhausted by minor knowledge or views.
One should practice throughout one's entire life, making the ultimate attainment one's standard. By all means, do not entertain the thought that it is easy.
The Bodhisattva said: "The *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is accomplished by the great power of your own minds; it is not brought about by others.

Now, as you practice the recollection of the Buddha, your state during the day and night cannot be made uniform. That distracted thoughts still intermittently interrupt the truth is entirely due to a lack of power in your application of the mind."
Gu Dingcheng requested instruction. The Bodhisattva said, "You have come to this hermitage wishing to rely on pure karma;
do you know how one may be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss? He replied, "By reciting the Buddha's name, one is reborn there. The Bodhisattva asked, "Do you know how to recite the Buddha's name?"
He immediately attained rebirth there. [The man] said, "I maintain the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction.
The Bodhisattva asked, "What is meant by 'single-mindedness and without distraction'? He was unable to answer. The Bodhisattva said, "I know that you are merely able to speak these words;
you are not necessarily able to practice in accordance with the Dharma. Listen attentively to my words. Good son, the mind is fundamentally without thought; thought follows after..."
Conceptualization gives rise to this; such conceptualization is false and leads to the cycle of birth and death.

You should now know that this single phrase, "Amitābha Buddha," does not arise from conceptualization, nor does it exist through recollection. It dwells neither within nor without, and possesses no marks or characteristics.
This is precisely the exhaustion of all deluded thoughts—the pure, subtle, and true body of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, which is neither one nor two. It is not...
One may discern it thus: for one who maintains such mindfulness, the afflictions and defilements are neither severed nor bound; they simply cease within a single mind.
Only when one has attained this single-mindedness can it be called "upholding the Name," and only then can it be called "single-mindedness without distraction.

When the merit of pure karma is perfected, one proceeds directly to the highest grade. He then prostrated himself and said: "Ordinary people of this turbid age possess shallow and inferior mental faculties."

"Since you have not yet deeply penetrated the ultimate principle, I shall further provide a detailed instruction for you. The Bodhisattva said, "You should now make a great vow, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).

Thereafter, with utmost sincerity and earnest compassion, recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, ensuring that the sound conditions the mind and the mind conditions the sound, so that sound and mind rely upon one another.
Just as a cat catches a mouse, do this for a long time without losing focus; then you will enter the correct [state]."
Recalling the samādhi and desiring to advance further, you should extensively consult wise teachers and widely inquire of the enlightened.
You must personally realize the subtle truth that the very mind is Buddha. You should now possess deep faith; be careful not to follow the common crowd who hear the teaching but do not accept it.
Furthermore, do not emulate those who are half-true and half-false, or those who harbor both doubt and faith; though they claim to have received the teaching, they lack it in reality.
She practiced with sincere devotion.
The Bodhisattva said to Chamo, "Why do you not diligently practice mindfulness of the Buddha? She replied, "Because I have many grandchildren, I constantly hold them in my arms;
I fear there may be impurity. The Bodhisattva said, "Do you mean that you practice mindfulness of the Buddha because you fear being defiled by impurity and thus incurring sin?"
If you do not know this and fail to recite the Buddha’s name, you will incur immeasurable transgressions. Do not deliberate over purity or impurity;
simply continue to recite.
Chen Yongshou asked for a definitive conclusion, and the Bodhisattva showed him this verse:
To restrain desire and refrain from anger is the method for preserving the body; To maintain self-restraint and tranquility is the method for being a master of one's house;
To marry according to one’s means is the method for reducing complications; To practice virtue and recite the Buddha’s name is the method for transcending the world.
By observing these four methods, one will ultimately attain thorough penetration.
Gu Shanji asked about how to ensure a virtuous end of life and the methods for practicing goodness. The Bodhisattva said:
"If you maintain a correct mind and perform correct deeds, you will attain a correct end of life. If you harbor a deviant mind and perform deviant deeds, you shall receive a deviant end of life.
As for the word 'goodness,' it can be practiced at any time and in any place; whether great or small matters, all are included. Furthermore—
Furthermore, observe the precept against killing and practice the release of captive creatures; according to your capacity, give alms to the poor and the suffering;

and maintain the recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha, dedicating the merit toward rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, without interruption day after day. If you can remain unchanged for three years in this manner, only then may you be granted the four characters: "Good-hearted One Who Practices Virtue."

The Bodhisattva showed Wu Xiu, saying: "In general, for one who cultivates pure karma, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, or during daily activities such as eating and drinking, it is appropriate to face west.
Thus, spiritual resonance will easily be achieved, and the faculties and their objects will easily reach maturity. Within the room, provide offerings to only one Buddha and one scripture;
there shall be only one incense burner, one table, one bed, and one chair. One must not allow any superfluous items to remain. This applies to the courtyard as well."

Sweep and cleanse the area so that one may walk back and forth without hindrance. One must ensure that this mind is free from even a single thread of attachment, forgetting all myriad concerns until it is utterly empty and void.
One should be unaware of the body, unaware of the world, and furthermore, unaware that what one is doing today is the practice of cultivation.
In this state, one draws closer to the Way day by day and becomes increasingly separated from the world; thus, one can advance toward it.
Turn toward pure karma. Indeed, at the time of your birth, you were cast forth with purity; you were cast forth with purity. Not a single trace of a root or a knot remains within your thoughts.
When the great limit arrives, you will be free and unburdened, without the manner of a woman or child who clings to body, family, or descendants.
Is this not the conduct of a great man? Therefore, I require that you focus your mind on this alone.
In the practice of cultivation, there is nothing else that causes stagnation; this is precisely the great pivotal point.

As for the method of cultivating purity, it does not go beyond the two characters "exclusive" and "diligent. To be exclusive means to perform no other task; to be diligent means to never waste a single moment.
When you rise this morning, immediately recite one scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and chant the name of Amitābha Buddha one thousand times.
Then, facing the Buddha, perform the dedication of merit and recite the "Text on Single-minded Taking Refuge. This text is chosen because its words are concise yet its meaning is complete.

This constitutes the practice for one session. If at the start of the day your body and mind are not yet settled, limit yourself to four sessions per day; once you are somewhat more settled, gradually increase.
Increase this to six sessions, and gradually increase it further until reaching twelve sessions, totaling twelve fascicles of scripture. Recite the names of the Buddhas twelve thousand times.
Furthermore, during the time of dedication (*pariṇāmana*), perform one hundred prostrations to the Buddha. Alternatively, these may be divided into four sessions;
this constitutes the daily routine. As for other work, there is no need to count it. Whether done silently or aloud, simply collect the mind and maintain focused mindfulness.

Furthermore, regarding the method of holding the Name: it is essential that every character and every phrase be accompanied by both voice and mind, without the slightest admixture of worldly thoughts.
Through long-term maturation, one will certainly attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī, sit upon a precious lotus flower, and ascend to the stage of non-retrogression.
If your remaining years have not yet come to an end, you may still serve as a guide for the fourfold assembly with what you have realized, thereby repaying the profound kindness of the Buddha.
If you follow each and every word of what I have taught, you will not fail the Bodhisattva Jue-ming, who showed you the right path and enabled you to leave the household life;
you will not fail your Preceptor Samadhi, who shaved your head and conferred upon you the Great Precepts.
