"This is no small matter. Do not harbor self-deprecation; be careful, be careful! The Bodhisattva Shishou said:
'It is excellent that you have previously held the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī and prayed for the secret empowerment of Avalokiteśvara, so that you may swiftly enter the Way.
However, you must not be consistently dilatory, allowing your resolve and practice to fail; you must apply yourself with all your days.'"
Proceeding with double the usual speed, from this day forward you shall fix a strict schedule and limit yourself to a set number of hours.
Cut off all social engagements and remain settled in a single room. Reciting one hundred fascicles [of the scripture] constitutes one period;

additionally, performing one fascicle of the repentance ritual established by Siming constitutes another period for purifying karmic obstructions and augmenting superior merit. Day and night are divided into six periods. By means of these...

Recite mantras during five periods of the day; at one period, perform prostrations and repentance; during the remaining times, sit in tranquility and cultivate dhyāna, entering deeply into inconceivable wisdom (*acintya-jñāna*).
What is meant by "inconceivable wisdom"? It is the thorough realization that there are no phenomena external to the mind, and that every phenomenon is without name.

Directly beneath this, not even a speck of dust can be established. In a single thought-moment, all is perfectly integrated (*pariniṣpanna*); it cannot be conceived by thought, nor can it be deliberated upon by discourse. Therefore, it is called "inconceivable."
This is the wisdom of contemplation. By relying on this sublime wisdom, the mind is gathered into subtlety; it gathers that which has no characteristic of being gathered.

That is to say, it gathers while there is nothing to be gathered, yet it is not obstructed by gathering. This is called the skillful gathering of the mind. Because the mind is thus gathered, there is no task that cannot be accomplished.
In short, there is no time or place where the mind does not flow into [the mantra]; this is the foundation for holding the mantra and gathering the mind.
Naturally, long-standing obstacles will melt away like ice, the concentrated mind will manifest with clarity, and one may attain the development of samādhi and realize the fundamental wondrous mind.

In this way, you will not have wasted the years and months in vain, and you can expect to advance on the Path within a fixed period. Otherwise, today and tomorrow will pass, and you will come [to regret it later].

Whether it be years or months from now, whether you act or do not act, whether you wish to advance or do not advance—after a hundred years, I shall still guarantee that your conduct remains exactly as it is before your eyes;
you will not be able to move even a single step. Be cautious! Exert yourself!

The Bodhisattva further showed Changshe, saying: "Those eight characters—'merely following human sentiments and striving to conform to worldly affairs'—have caused you to miss the great matter of your entire life.
At this moment, it is by no means the time for dragging along companions or passing the days with idle chatter.

Since your path of practice is not yet complete and impermanence arrives with great speed, you must urgently withdraw from public view and conceal your brilliance, directing your mind single-mindedly toward [the Way]."
The Way must not be mistaken again.
Dabeng took the precepts and left the household life. The Bodhisattva instructed him, saying: "Since you have entered the monastic life at an advanced age, you must not study miscellaneous matters.
Recite only the Amitābha Sūtra; daily, chant the Buddha’s name twelve thousand times. Start from a small number and gradually increase it until it is truly and authentically so."
Be earnest! Seek birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; this is the method by which one thing accomplished settles all others.

Do not follow the worldly and foolish crowd who engage in lofty talk and grandiloquent discourse, prattling on about "sacrificing the flesh" or "purifying the mind. When they see someone reciting the Buddha’s name, they dismiss them all at once as being of no account.
Yet when their own conduct is examined, it does not even match that of an illiterate man from a three-family village or a commoner at the crossroads.
A beggar who merely recites the *Sanguan jing* (Scripture on the Three Officials) has wasted his time and missed the great matter because, in his daily life,
he delighted in speaking of Chan without grasping its essential subtlety, and perhaps lacked deep faith in the Pure Land and the practice of earnestly reciting the Buddha’s name;
it is for this reason that I have composed this treatise.
The Bodhisattva further instructed Wuxiu, saying: "The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* consists of twelve fascicles and contains twelve thousand names of Buddhas.
Do not increase them, nor do you decrease them; simply follow my practice. As for the recitation of the sutra, it must be even and pure—neither lax nor hurried, neither too fast nor too slow.
Regarding the invocation of the Buddha’s name, every sound and every thought must be focused—neither stilted nor wavering, neither floating nor sinking."
As for "mindfulness of departure": when reaching the "thousandfold dedication," it is not merely a matter of reciting the old text once;

one must, from within one's own heart, give rise to a truly great *bodhicitta* vow. With utmost sincerity and earnestness, one universally vows that all sentient beings may together be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, while one’s own mind remains unattached, equal to empty space—this is called dedication. Furthermore, during the time of sitting in stillness:
One should turn back to observe and investigate deeply: the Buddha is none other than one’s own mind; this very mind is the Buddha. There is no need to seek it externally.
Abide according to the nature of the mind—without subject or object. Contemplate thus with single-minded focus, without a second thought. This is called the cultivation of samādhi.

Be careful not to lose the physical form or let the mind die, nor fall into the views and knowledge of external māras. Having sat in meditation for a period of time, one should then rise and practice walking meditation.

Furthermore, there is a specific sequence for recitation. If one proceeds in a frantic and hurried manner, rushing through it in a single breath with the thought that one can thus complete the day's liturgy, this reflects a mind of negligence and superficiality; it is not true cultivation.
Generally speaking, if a student of the Way does not follow the clear instructions of their spiritual mentor, they will certainly labor in vain without benefit and will surely fail before long.
Be careful! Be careful! Furthermore, regarding the descriptions of the adornments of the pure land and its inhabitants found in the various sutras, you must explain and recite them with clarity.

Should the pure land manifest before you while sitting, walking, or performing prostrations and recitations, you will be able to recognize it immediately and not be deluded by it as a strange or extraordinary phenomenon.
The Bodhisattva pointed out to Chen Dashen, saying: "Your aspiration for the Way has increased, yet your worldly thoughts have not diminished.
All worldly notions of self and other, of fame and profit, and of anger and joy do not merely manifest through your physical conduct."
At the outset, you were entangled in the net of worldly dust; yet, if even a slight trace remains upon the mind, it immediately becomes a cause and condition for obstructing the Path.

You must understand this clearly. You need only pay homage to Amitābha with your body, recite the name of Amitābha with your mouth, and contemplate Amitābha with your mind, without allowing even a fraction of other thoughts to intervene.
Thus, you shall attain complete purification, break through the net of worldly dust, and be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
"O Countryman, you must understand this clearly.
Someone asked, "What about for a lifetime? The Bodhisattva said, "Are you asking about a lifetime? Here, I have no dharma that cuts off the end of a lifetime as its cause.
Even though I have practiced through kalpas, I have never learned such a thing. However, you too are far too—"
Foolishness! To spend one's entire life in this manner—what benefit is there in questioning others? Why do you not ask yourself:
"My hair has turned white, my face is wrinkled, my body has grown frail, and impermanence is about to arrive.
Before King Yama, how will I manage to utter even a single word or phrase in response? How can I avoid being bound in shackles and chains? This matter, you...
"Why do you not ask?
The monk Falyuan was about to establish a period for performing the Maitreya-Amitābha repentance ritual (*mítuó chàn*). He had previously come to seek instruction. The Bodhisattva said:

"The Amitābha Repentance was compiled by the recent Chan Master Ciyun. It also encompasses both the phenomenal and the noumenal aspects of single-mindedness. Phenomenal single-mindedness consists in focusing exclusively on—"
First point: If the four characteristics do not arise and one is as tranquil as empty space, this is called "one mind in principle. This one mind is difficult to attain;

therefore, externally one diligently practices the method of repentance to eliminate past obstacles, and internally one relies on principle to cultivate contemplation, gradually leading to the attainment of one mind.

Once you have attained single-mindedness, what concern could there be about being unable to enter the Way? At this stage, do not concern yourself with whether it is for your own sake or for the sake of the donor;
nor should you worry about whether it will last long or not. You need only sweep away habitual tendencies and thoroughly cleanse the body and mind.
Do not rest until you have attained samādhi; this is my vow. That is all. Furthermore, although you may follow the sequence there, it is not the ground for true cultivation.
If you truly wish to practice, cast aside all external conditions. Let your single bowl depend upon the ten directions and your single body depend upon the great earth.
With sincere and earnest resolve, seek liberation from birth and death; this alone is the correct path.

Regarding the practice of the Dharma: if you spend a period of three years in earnest repentance yet allow worldly affairs to interfere, hoping thereby to accomplish pure karma and transcend birth and death, it is like seeking satiety by inhaling wind and swallowing mist—this is an impossibility in this world.
Do not harbor such great delusions, lest you die of cold and hunger.
When the Imperial Army first descended upon the Three Wu regions, lake pirates suddenly erupted, and the entire city fled in panic.

After a long time, when order was restored and people gradually began to gather again, the Bodhisattva showed them [a vision] and said: "Will you not be struck with terror by the upheaval of the thirteenth day of the sixth month?
You should know that all of this is because, since beginningless kalpas, you have been unable to cultivate goodness and have extensively created evil karma; therefore, birth after birth..."
Life after life, they have not been free from this calamity, just as during the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, when eight people were scattered by military chaos;

today, once again they encounter a military upheaval and flee with no place to hide. This demonstrates that sentient beings are unable to transcend the three realms of existence and attain the state of non-arising.
Ultimately, the karmic retribution of causes and conditions is difficult to evade even by a fraction. That you have not yet died is itself a great peril.
The fruits of karma across the three periods of time are truly startling and terrifying; yet you still do not single-mindedly strive for the Way to escape the wheel of suffering at an early date.
"Regarding the next life and future rebirths, we do not yet know what lies ahead. Alas! Alas!
The Bodhisattva said to Shen Yuanhui: "In general, those who cultivate the Pure Land most dread being 'intermingled' (jiázá).
What is meant by being intermingled? It refers to reciting sutras, chanting mantras, organizing assemblies, and also taking pleasure in discussing trivial matters."
To speak of Chan while also discussing matters of fortune and misfortune, or visions of gods and ghosts, is to intermingle [diverse concerns].
Once there is such intermingling, the mind will not be single-minded. When the mind is not single-minded, it will be difficult to see the Buddha and attain rebirth.
Otherwise, you will have spent your entire life in vain. From now on, do nothing at all;
simply and resolutely hold fast to the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha," vowing to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. When your practice has matured over time, you will finally avoid error.
I shall grant you a verse; follow it and put it into practice.
The single phrase of Amitābha is the dhāraṇī that encompasses all phenomena. Sound and mind rely upon one another;
as you recite it, it is ever-present here. This response and resonance is inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva said to Dingkai: "Since you have encountered great peril and fortunately escaped, from this day forward you must reflect deeply upon this."
The past is gone; sever its future transgressions. No longer harbor a restless mind, nor compete with others in spirit or display your willful cleverness, thereby bringing calamity upon yourself.
Now I shall establish a name for you: Kai. What is Kai? It means compassion and benevolence. Establish yourself through compassion; reach out to others through benevolence.
If you gain fame and merit, do not be overly joyful; if you fail, do not be overly distressed. Devote yourself solely to cultivating a virtuous mind and remain steadfast.
"Excellent conduct! It is merely to respond with gratitude to the four debts of gratitude.
At one time, a Bodhisattva descended upon the Dharma assembly. There were over thirty people among the officials and commoners whose doubts regarding their resolve had not yet been resolved;

they all came to seek counsel from the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva took pity on this multitude, noting that although they shared the same sincere devotion, they did not recognize the correct path of cultivation.

He then offered this instruction: "The assembly gathered today may be called one of great affinity. However, if I were to preach the Buddha-dharma to you, it would not accord with what you have studied;
I fear you would find it difficult to believe. It would be better to cite a single passage from a secular classic or a Confucian text to converse with you all.
Perhaps you might gain faith in one or two sentences. As the *Zhongyong* says: 'Some practice it with ease, while others practice it for profit.'"
And they practice it—some practicing it with effort. Looking at it today, let alone speak of peace and benefit, even that which is practiced with effort cannot be sustained.
It is just as when you yourselves, after meeting me, once resolved to strive for goodness, yet suddenly abandoned it, or gradually fell into negligence and indolence. Why is this? Its cause...
Why is this so? It is simply because one views the single word "goodness" too laxly, thinking that practicing goodness yields no merit and is less effective than committing evil.
One fails to realize that if practicing goodness truly yielded no merit, why would the sages and worthies of antiquity never commit even the slightest bit of evil?
Rather, they exerted all their strength and heart in goodness, determined to carry it through to completion.
The twelve links are fully complete. If committing evil were truly effective, for what reason have the benevolent men and gentlemen of antiquity not sought only such efficacy?
On the contrary, they performed deeds that yielded no worldly reward.
Furthermore, we see with our own eyes that those who commit evil may enjoy temporary advantage, yet in the end, how many achieve a favorable conclusion, a favorable end, or a favorable reputation?

Thus descendants prolong their lineage through the generations. It is also like a small child in this world who, upon hearing of a good person, immediately knows to praise them—is this not because there is great benefit in doing good?

Upon hearing of an evil person, they immediately feel resentment—is this not because there is no great benefit in doing evil? This matter is extremely easy to understand; it is not something beyond your comprehension.

It is not that you lack intelligence; it is simply that you do not know how to attain it. It is merely because you cannot apply your whole heart toward the good that you fail to examine things closely at times.
Therefore, in your daily life, you feel the need to announce to others every time you give away a single coin, and you likewise feel the need to proclaim every fine word you have heard.
You act entirely from the outside, never truly internalizing or understanding these things.
When the Great Sage and Great Sages applied their minds with such urgency to their own persons,
they realized there was no flavor [of self-interest] therein and cast it aside. If you all today truly employ a sincere heart and perform sincere deeds,
without a single trace of delusive thoughts or covetousness intervening, then remain composed, finding joy in Heaven and accepting your fate, guarding that which resides within yourself.

One will see that there is a lifelong path upon which one can pray; in the end, the fortunes and misfortunes of the Five Elements and Eight Characters (Wuxing Bazi) may be divined, and one will be able to pursue or avoid good and bad fortune, gain and loss.
Naturally, no calamity will fail to be dispelled, and no blessing will fail to arrive.
One’s Way will increase with the times, and one’s virtue will accumulate with each year. It will not be difficult to become a sage or a worthy. This is your certain future.
This is the reality of things. Therefore it is said that when success is achieved, they are one and the same;
conversely, those who act without restraint will become petty men in life and withered plants after death—is this not to be lamented?

When the Bodhisattva had finished speaking these words and remained silent, the assembly still waited expectantly with uplifted faces. Some even prostrated themselves again to offer prayers. The Bodhisattva...
Sakyamuni said, "How profound is the folly of you, the assembly! Having heard such words, you have failed to give rise to a mind of aspiration or even a thought of reflection;
you merely ask about the matters of children and family within your own breasts, and then stop."
Alas, alas! Yet the Bodhisattva’s great compassion is inexhaustible; he shall further relate some ancient tales to awaken you from your deluded dreams.
First, as for those who study the Way: if their emotions are not upright, their nature will become estranged; if their minds are not firm, their virtue will be deficient.
Often they are cautious for a moment only to change in an instant. Such as these are said to have failed in their cultivation.
This current of the world is difficult to enter upon the Path; it is not that the Sage grew weary of instructing others and therefore abandoned them.
Those among the multitude who possess discernment should reflect on this: first, there are still many in the world who are intelligent and striving for spiritual advancement.

Yet, being obstructed by the view of self-righteousness, they fail to become great vessels. For when a person is self-righteous, they will certainly refuse to humble their mind and seek correction from those who possess the Way.
Those with whom such a person regularly associates and interacts are invariably a class of mediocre and inferior individuals who praise one another;
consequently, whenever there is anything they do, they cannot hear of their faults face-to-face, and thus their virtue and achievements are surely ruined.
Among the assembly, those with discernment reflect upon this: First, worldly people are greedy for gain and strive solely for forceful acquisition.
They do not realize that even in the earning of a single coin, there is still the matter of fate; how much more so regarding the great matters of fame, achievement, wealth, and nobility!
They say, "If my own wisdom and strength can seek these things, then what use would the azure heavens or the majestic deities have? Even if one were to seek them through forceful means—
It is obtained through the convergence of one's destiny and fortune, not by employing such tedious mental artifice;

it is granted by Heaven out of compassion. Thus, those who strive and seek after it will find only humiliation rather than honor, failure rather than attainment, the calamity of self-destruction rather than the merit of benefiting others, the disaster of impairing virtue rather than the blessing of advancing toward goodness.

"Heaven has grown weary of him, and the spirits have abandoned him. Those among the assembly who possess discernment reflect upon this: first, there is no greater kindness in the world than that of one's parents.
While they are still present, they are living Buddhas before one's hall; once they have passed away, it is still possible to offer them posthumous requital.
Consider for a moment: from where does this body come? By what means does it grow? Yet, one is unable to return to the source and seek its origin.
They exhaust their hearts and strength, reverently serving and obeying [their parents], yet they go so far as to harbor resentment toward their parents without regard for them;

they seek their own benefit for their wives and children while failing to support them; furthermore, there are even those who do not recognize when their parents are ill and do not bury them when they die.
If one responds to a single word with retaliation as if they were an ordinary person, such individuals are inferior even to birds and beasts. Alas!
To be human yet inferior to birds and beasts—how terrifying! Let those among the assembly who possess discernment reflect upon this.
Someone wished to seek an official post and asked whether it could be obtained. The Bodhisattva said, "As for the matter of holding office, you must not even entertain such thoughts.

You must know that what is called 'letters' (wen) refers to mastery of the classics and histories; what is called 'military' (wu) refers to proficiency in strategy and tactics; what is called 'courage' (yong) refers to physical strength exceeding that of others;
and what is called 'talent' (cai) refers to intelligence surpassing the masses. Reflect upon this yourself: do you possess even one of these? If [you lack] the four..."
Among these, they lack even one. To seek office is nothing more than plotting for luck; to plot for luck means that one’s intentions are already impure from the start.
